text: Meridian Regional Health runs four hospitals, and its Patient Scheduling system handles thousands of patient appointments a day across all of them. Despite being flagged by clinical operations as one of the most disruptive systems to lose, it has never had a single CMDB entry. This four-lesson capstone builds that record for real — scoping the service, modeling it, applying everything this course has taught, and closing with a governance plan.

Leadership's ask is specific: an accurate view of what infrastructure actually supports Patient Scheduling, the ability to run real impact analysis before any planned maintenance touches that infrastructure, and ongoing confidence that the data stays correct long after this initial build — not a one-time snapshot that quietly goes stale within six months.

Chapter Three's Business Service and Technical Service split applies directly. Patient Scheduling itself is the Business Service — the thing patients and schedulers experience, and what leadership asks about the moment there's an outage. Underneath it will sit Patient Scheduling Application Service, the Technical Service made of real, physical and virtual infrastructure: application servers, a database, a load balancer, and the scheduling application itself, none of which exist in the CMDB yet.

Patient Scheduling also exchanges data with Meridian's Electronic Health Records platform, but that EHR system is already its own Business Service, with its own owner and its own CMDB footprint elsewhere. This capstone will not re-model it. Lesson 24 adds exactly one relationship showing where that handoff happens, and nothing more — the kind of explicit scope boundary that keeps a first CMDB build from sprawling into a mess nobody can finish or maintain.

The plan for the rest of this chapter: Lesson 24 builds the actual configuration items supporting Patient Scheduling and the relationships connecting them. Lesson 25 maps that technical service up to the business service, decides where Discovery takes over maintaining the infrastructure CIs, configures identification rules against duplicates, and checks the result against the CMDB Health Dashboard. Lesson 26 closes with a real, named governance plan.

With the service scoped, the boundary drawn, and the plan set, it's time to build. Next: modeling Patient Scheduling's actual application, servers, database, and load balancer — and documenting exactly how they depend on each other.
